previous_disclosures.summary: The company is required to submit periodic resolution and recovery plans to the FRB and FDIC, with G-SIBs submitting full or targeted plans every two years. The 2023 full plan was submitted in June 2023, with the next targeted submission due by July 1, 2025. Failure to remediate plan shortcomings may result in stricter requirements. comparisons.peer_topic: U.S. Resolution Plan Requirements and Credibility Risks
comparisons.peer_summary: As a BHC with over $250 billion in assets, the Corporation must submit a resolution plan every two years for orderly resolution without government assistance; if deemed not credible, the Federal Reserve and FDIC may impose stricter capital, leverage, or liquidity requirements.
comparisons.comparison: Both Goldman Sachs and Bank of America, as U.S. G-SIBs/BHCs, are subject to the requirement to submit resolution plans every two years for rapid and orderly resolution without government assistance. A key difference is that Goldman Sachs disclosed in June 2024 that regulators identified a specific shortcoming in its 2023 plan requiring a targeted 2025 plan, whereas Bank of America's disclosure focuses on the general regulatory framework and the potential consequences of a non-credible plan (stricter capital/liquidity requirements) without citing a recent specific regulatory shortcoming.

sentences.text: We are required by the FRB and the FDIC to submit a periodic plan for our rapid and orderly resolution in the event of material financial distress or failure (resolution plan).
The FRB and FDIC require U.S. G-SIBs to submit resolution plans every two years (alternating between submissions of full plans and targeted plans that include only select information).

In June 2024, the FRB and the FDIC provided feedback on our 2023 resolution plan and identified one shortcoming, other areas for additional focus to address resolution readiness and additional information required to be included in our 2025 resolution plan.

As a BHC with greater than $250 billion of assets, every two years the Corporation is required by the Federal Reserve and the FDIC to submit a plan for a rapid and orderly resolution in the event of material financial distress or failure.

Such resolution plan is intended to be a detailed roadmap for the orderly resolution of the BHC, including the continued operations or solvent wind down of its material entities, pursuant to the U.S. Bankruptcy Code under one or more hypothetical scenarios assuming no extraordinary government assistance.

If both the Federal Reserve and the FDIC determine that the BHC's plan is not credible, the Federal Reserve and the FDIC may jointly impose more stringent capital, leverage or liquidity requirements or restrictions on growth, activities or operations.

comparisons.peer_summary: Citi's disclosure controls and procedures are designed to ensure information required under the Securities Exchange Act is recorded, processed, and reported within SEC time periods, including accumulation and communication to the CEO and CFO for timely decisions.
comparisons.comparison: While Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley focus on 'resolution plans' for failure/distress, Citi's disclosed text in this specific candidate refers to 'disclosure controls and procedures' for SEC reporting accuracy. However, as a peer in the same regulatory taxonomy, it is relevant to note that Citi is also subject to resolution planning requirements under the same laws, but the provided text does not contain comparable resolution plan data, only general disclosure control definitions. The comparison highlights that while the regulatory obligation exists for all, the specific disclosure content regarding resolution plan status (shortcomings, dates) is absent in this Citi candidate compared to the detailed GS/MS disclosures.

sentences.text: We are required by the FRB and the FDIC to submit a periodic plan for our rapid and orderly resolution in the event of material financial distress or failure (resolution plan).

Citi's disclosure controls and procedures are designed to ensure that information required to be disclosed under the Securities Exchange Act of 1934, as amended, is recorded, processed, summarized and reported within the time periods specified in the SEC's rules and forms, including without limitation that information required to be disclosed by Citi in its SEC filings is accumulated and communicated to management, including the Chief Executive Officer (CEO) and Chief Financial Officer (CFO), as appropriate, to allow for timely decisions regarding required disclosure.

comparisons.peer_topic: CCAR Stress Testing and SCB Requirements
comparisons.peer_summary: JPMorgan Chase is subject to annual supervisory stress tests under the CCAR framework and must submit an annual capital plan, with the Federal Reserve using severely adverse scenario results to determine the Stress Capital Buffer (SCB); the firm is required to file its 2025 CCAR submission by April 5, 2025, with final SCB requirements effective October 1, 2025, amid pending changes to the framework and legal challenges.
comparisons.comparison: Both Goldman Sachs and JPMorgan Chase are subject to rigorous Federal Reserve supervision and planning requirements. However, the specific topics differ: Goldman Sachs focuses on 'resolution plans' (living wills) under the Dodd-Frank Act for orderly failure, whereas JPMorgan's disclosed candidate focuses on 'CCAR stress testing' and capital planning. Both involve the Federal Reserve and are critical regulatory compliance items for G-SIBs, but one addresses insolvency strategy (GS) while the other addresses capital adequacy under stress scenarios (JPM).

sentences.text: We are required by the FRB and the FDIC to submit a periodic plan for our rapid and orderly resolution in the event of material financial distress or failure (resolution plan).

As a large BHC, JPMorganChase is subject to supervisory stress testing administered by the Federal Reserve as part of the Federal Reserve's annual Comprehensive Capital Analysis and Review ("CCAR") framework.

The Firm must conduct annual company-run stress tests and must also submit an annual capital plan to the Federal Reserve, taking into account the results of separate stress tests designed by each of the Firm and the Federal Reserve.

comparisons.peer_summary: The firm is required to submit biennial resolution plans outlining a strategy for orderly resolution under the U.S. Bankruptcy Code, with a targeted plan due in July 2025, and annual recovery plans. Domestic and foreign subsidiaries, including U.S. bank subsidiaries, have their own resolution and recovery planning requirements with submissions due in 2026. The firm may be subject to the FDIC's orderly liquidation authority in cases of extraordinary distress, which grants the FDIC broad powers, with an expected preference for a Single Point of Entry (SPOE) strategy. The filing cross-references specific Risk Factors and MD&A sections for further details on these disclosures.
comparisons.comparison: Both Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley explicitly disclose their upcoming submission of a 'targeted' resolution plan in July 2025, contrasting with the prior 'full' plan submission. Both firms also detail the separate requirement for their U.S. bank subsidiaries to submit resolution plans to the FDIC. Goldman Sachs specifies its bank subsidiary's next full submission is due July 2026, while Morgan Stanley generally notes that its U.S. Bank Subsidiaries submit plans every two years with interim targeted information, though it does not specify the exact 2026 date for Morgan Stanley's bank subsidiary in this excerpt.

sentences.text: The FRB and FDIC require U.S. G-SIBs to submit resolution plans every two years (alternating between submissions of full plans and targeted plans that include only select information).
IDIs with $100 billion or more in total assets, including GS Bank USA, are required to submit full resolution plans biennially.
GS Bank USA's next required full submission is due by July 1, 2026.
Our next resolution plan submission will be a targeted resolution plan in July 2025.

The FDIC currently requires certain insured depository institutions ("IDI"), including our U.S. Bank Subsidiaries, to submit full resolution plans every two years and interim targeted information at certain times between full resolution plan submissions that describe the IDI's strategy for a rapid and orderly resolution in the event of material financial distress or failure of the IDI.

Submission of interim targeted information by our U.S. Bank Subsidiaries generally will not be required during a year which the Parent Company is required to submit a resolution plan to the Federal Reserve and FDIC.
